content.comment_body: I had several [product_name] controllers networked together using our [company_name] network. There are about 12 people on my office's local network, with roughly 20 more logging in remotely. Although the controllers operated without issue, the rest of the network became unstable and required a router reset. Is it common for network problems to occur when these controllers are connected to a company network?

Hello, I have six [product_name] units with [article_no] version set up on my home network, which includes two WiFi routers and a standard router. There are five people using computers and mobile devices, and I frequently open network tunnels. One WiFi router needs to be restarted daily. After monitoring traffic using Wireshark, everything appeared normal. I suspect the issue is the router's buffer due to the controllers constantly communicating with each other, 24/7. The other two routers do not experience this issue. For my next upgrade, I plan to replace this router ([company_name] NETGEAR). As a temporary solution, I used a spare relay from a nearby controller to power the router, and a loop between two controllers monitors the network. If a small timer isn't reset within 30 seconds, the router is powered off for 20 seconds to restart it, resulting in a maximum of a 60-second network outage for part of the network.

analysis.insight_summary: Users encounter network instability when using multiple [product_name] controllers (such as [article_no] versions) on typical office or home networks. The controllers work reliably, but their continuous network communication seems to overwhelm routers with limited buffer capacity, leading to frequent router failures and the need for resets. This affects other network users and disrupts overall network performance.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect [product_name] controllers to integrate seamlessly into standard office or home networks, without triggering network disruptions or router failures.
